title_original: At Paris Photo, Women Shoot First
excerpt_original: At the Grand Palais, Paris gallery Anne de Villepoix honors Carolee Schneemann, Martha Rosler, Judit Kele, Iris Brosch, and Olivia Crowe Reavey — five trailblazers of feminist performance photography, the women who cleared the way for Marina Abramović, Orlan, and Sophie Calle.…

blocks.text: Shoot, aim, frame, reload: photography has spoken the gunsmith’s language from the very start. As early as 1882, the physiologist Étienne-Jules Marey was shouldering his chronophotographic rifle to capture birds in flight, and Henri Cartier-Bresson defined the medium as the art of “putting one’s head, one’s eye and one’s heart on the same axis.”

The American essayist Susan Sontag saw in the photographic act a form of “predation one click away,” recalls the philosopher and art critic Philippe Godin in the essay accompanying the hang. Women were long its game of choice. The five artists on stand A42 have turned the rifle around: in their hands, he writes, the photograph “is no longer a mere still image to be looked at; it becomes the extension of an action.”

First on the rope, Carolee Schneemann (1939-2019) started out as a painter in a New York where Action Painting was a “boys’ club” and the brush a virile attribute. Her first coup came in Paris, in May 1964: Meat Joy , a pagan liturgy in which eight partially nude performers anointed one another with paint and passed raw fish, chickens, and sausages from arm to arm, under strict orders never to let the meat touch the floor. In 1975, in Interior Scroll , standing on a table, she drew from her vagina a scroll of paper and declaimed its text as it unspooled.

blocks.caption: Up To and Including her limits, 1976 © Carolee Schneemann, courtesy Galerie Anne de Villepoix

blocks.text: The following year, suspended naked in a tree surgeon’s harness, she traced on the walls whatever her swaying dictated, for Up To and Including Her Limits , whose installation has belonged to MoMA since 2012. “A body utterly distended, strapped in, has something rather violent about it,” concedes Pierre Henry Gamelin, art advisor and founder of the agency PHG Art Advisory, our guide through the booth.

Martha Rosler’s scissors slice into the same established order. The New Yorker, born in Brooklyn in 1943 and loyal to the gallery since 1997, clipped rumps and breasts from men’s magazines and shelved them in a refrigerator: Cold Meat I (1972), cold cuts to eat in or take out. In the video Semiotics of the Kitchen (1975), a cooking-show parody recited utensil by utensil, whisk and cleaver rise to the rank of edged weapons, and the cooking lesson, in Philippe Godin’s words, turns into an “alphabet of rage.”

The retort from the stove arrives from the East. In The Artist in the Kitchen (1979), the Hungarian Judit Kele cooks fire itself, flaming wooden spoon in hand. “Is a woman made only to cook? Is a woman made only to stay home?” translates Pierre Henry Gamelin, standing before the image at Paris Photo. That same year, at the Museum of Fine Arts in Budapest, the artist spent three days occupying the spot left vacant by El Greco’s Annunciation , then on loan to the Prado in Madrid, under the watch of an armed policeman: “I am a work of art,” proclaimed this child of a communist Hungary that enforced anonymity.

blocks.caption: Sexual and artistic freedom, 1995 © Iris Brosch, courtesy Galerie Anne de Villepoix
The Artist in the kitchen, 1979 © Judit Kele, courtesy Galerie Anne de Villepoix

blocks.text: She then pushed the needle further still. Through a classified ad in the daily Libération , she invited men to marry her and had the suitors bid at the Paris Biennale. A French collector, the highest bidder, carried off the piece, wedding in Budapest included, under the gaze of plainclothes policemen. Five years of married life as an art object proved sufficient: in 1985 she divorced, took her bow with a farewell performance, and reinvented herself as a filmmaker.

In the meantime, another outcast found refuge in Paris. The American researcher Shere Hite had rattled her country with The Hite Report (1976), a survey of thousands of women on orgasm and masturbation, and one of the thirty best-selling books in the world during the 1980s. “Puritan America couldn’t take it,” Pierre Henry Gamelin offers. A commission from Elle magazine brought her, in 1991, before the lens of Iris Brosch, a German-Austrian fashion photographer newly settled in the French capital. Until Hite’s death in 2020, the two friends composed hundreds of images of Madonnas in pearls and baroque frames, among them the series “The Bleeding Madonna,” which transfigures menstruation in the manner of the Pre-Raphaelites. Several prints, hand-solarized between 1991 and 1995, still carry the researcher’s signature on the back.

blocks.text: One blind spot remains: the male nude as seen by a woman, homoerotic photography, from Robert Mapplethorpe to Herb Ritts, having sung it in every key. Olivia Crowe Reavey, 28, trained at the Rhode Island School of Design and now in the MFA program at Yale, steps in without blinking. Her models, men and mostly naked, lend themselves to “an awkward dance whose choreography neither photographer nor subject knows”; intimidation switches sides, and the balance of power is renegotiated. Where her elders turned the rifle around, the young American takes it apart: defused by humor and abstraction, the phallus no longer lays down the law, and penises at rest, like the hollows of armpits, accede to the dignity of landscape. The enchantment is sealed in the darkroom, by way of incisions, scratches, Vaseline, and developments stretched to the point of distortion: “a witchcraft of photography in the service of a joyful feminism,” Philippe Godin applauds.

blocks.text: Half a century separates the “alphabet of rage” from this “joyful feminism”: the pioneers’ fury has learned to take its pleasure. And the shooting is now the kind done in a darkroom: women shoot first, and their prints land square in the heart.

“Photography Put to the Test of Feminist Performance,” with Iris Brosch, Judit Kele, Olivia Crowe Reavey, Martha Rosler, and Carolee Schneemann, Galerie Anne de Villepoix at Paris Photo , Grand Palais, stand A42, through November 15, 2026.
